title: Scalable long-distance quantum fan-out gates with reduced resource overhead
abstract: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are essential for distributed quantum computation and scalable quantum networks. We propose an efficient scheme for implementing an $n$-qubit fan-out gate $C^n$ (also known as a controlled-NOT-$\cdots$-NOT gate) across spatially separated parties. Our protocol requires only a pre-shared $n$-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, $n$ local controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates, and feed-forward operations, thereby reducing both the CNOT and Hadamard gate counts by $(n-2)$ when compared with the standard decomposition-based approach. We further develop two optical architectures to implement the heralded and post-selected $n$-photon fan-out gates, respectively. These schemes require fewer single photons resources and achieve higher success probabilities than their decomposition-based counterparts, representing significant improvements. The results indicate that our approach is experimentally feasible and pave the way toward practical long-distance quantum computation.
summary: This paper presents an optimized scheme for implementing the crucial $n$-qubit quantum fan-out gate ($C_n$) required for quantum networks. By leveraging pre-shared GHZ states, the authors drastically reduce the required number of gates compared to existing methods. They further demonstrate the experimental feasibility of this scheme using advanced linear optical architectures for photonic qubits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need for scalable, long-distance quantum fan-out gates ($C_n$) necessary for distributed quantum computation and quantum networks.
main_result: The authors propose an efficient protocol using pre-shared GHZ states and local CNOT gates, significantly reducing gate counts compared to standard decomposition methods. They also developed high-success-probability optical architectures for heralded and post-selected gates.
method: The work compares a standard decomposition-based approach against a novel scheme utilizing pre-shared multi-qubit entangled states (GHZ) and local operations, implemented both abstractly (qubit model) and physically (linear optics/photons).
model_or_system: The primary focus is on implementing the $n$-qubit fan-out gate ($C_n$) using photonic qubits encoded in polarization states. The protocols are demonstrated using linear optics components like Polarizing Beam Splitters (PBSs) and Half-Wave Plates (HWPs).
key_observables: Gate counts (CNOT, Hadamard), success probabilities (e.g., $\left( rac{1}{2}ight)^{3n-1}$), and fidelity under noise.
important_parameters: The efficiency calculations involve parameters like $\eta_s$ (per-photon survival efficiency) and $\eta_d$ (detection efficiency), which are crucial for assessing experimental feasibility.
main_assumptions: The efficiency calculations rely on specific, state-of-the-art experimental parameters for photon sources and detectors. The protocol assumes the availability of a pre-shared $n$-qubit GHZ state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum circuits for the standard decomposition-based $C_n$ gate and the proposed efficient $C_n$ gate using ancillary GHZ states. Another figure details the linear optics setup for the heralded $C_3$ gate using PBSs and HWPs.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of scalable long-distance $C_n$ gates. It then details the resource reduction achieved by using GHZ states over standard decomposition. Finally, it translates these concepts into concrete, high-fidelity optical architectures for heralded and post-selected gates.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and quantum information, as it provides concrete, resource-optimized blueprints for building the core components needed for large-scale quantum networking using photons.
